title: Structure of the simultaneous parameter-root algebra over a strict local ring
statement:
Let $R$ be a strictly henselian regular Noetherian local ring, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ and residue field $k$ [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology, def-weil-regular-scheme, def-weil-residue-field]. Let $t_1,\ldots,t_r\in\mathfrak m$, for $r\geq0$, extend to a regular system of parameters [def-weil-pbc-regular-system-of-parameters]. Let $n\geq1$ be invertible in $R$, and let $\zeta\in R^\times$ satisfy $\zeta^n=1$ and $1-\zeta^a\in R^\times$ for $1\leq a<n$. Put
$$B=R[x_1,\ldots,x_r]/(x_1^n-t_1,\ldots,x_r^n-t_r),\qquad f=\prod_i t_i,$$
using multivariate polynomial rings [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. Then $B$ is a strictly henselian regular local domain, its residue field map $k\to B/\mathfrak m_B$ is an isomorphism, and it is free as an $R$-module on $x^a=\prod_i x_i^{a_i}$ with $0\leq a_i<n$ (that is, every element of $B$ has a unique $R$-linear expansion in those monomials). In particular $R\to B$ is injective. Write $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ and $E=\operatorname{Frac}(B)$ [def-pc-field-extension]. The extension $E/K$ is finite Galois (finite and separable [def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension], with the minimal polynomial of each element splitting into linear factors over $E$), has degree $n^r$, and the homomorphism
$$(\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z)^r\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}_K(E),\qquad h(x_i)=\zeta^{h_i}x_i,$$
is an isomorphism. These rotations preserve $B$. The map $\operatorname{Spec}B[1/f]\to\operatorname{Spec}R[1/f]$ is finite etale [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-ring-localization-away, def-weil-finite-integral-morphism, def-weil-etale-morphism]. Empty products are $1$; when $r=0$ one has $B=R$, $E=K$ and the trivial group.

proof.text: Put $B_j=R[x_1,\ldots,x_j]/(x_1^n-t_1,\ldots,x_j^n-t_j)$, with $B_0=R$. The universal properties of polynomial and quotient rings identify $B_j$ with $B_{j-1}[T]/(T^n-t_j)$, sending $T$ to $x_j$: both represent tuples of roots of the same equations. Apply the monic-quotient power-basis theorem at each stage. Induction on $j$ gives the unique expansion $\sum_{0\leq a_i<n}c_a x^a$ over $R$, since expanding first in $x_j$ and then expanding each coefficient is unique. In particular $B=B_r$ is finite free of rank $n^r$, and the coefficient of the basis element $1$ proves that $R\to B$ is injective. Finite-algebra integrality and Noetherianity apply to this finite $R$-module, so $B$ is integral over $R$ and Noetherian.

source.place: Tag 04GG (lemma-characterize-henselian), monic finite-free quotient calculation in the proof; Tag 00GK (lemma-finite-is-integral); Tag 00FN (lemma-Noetherian-permanence).

proof.text: The same presentation modulo $\mathfrak m$ gives $B/\mathfrak m B=k[x_1,\ldots,x_r]/(x_1^n,\ldots,x_r^n)$. Every prime in this ring contains every $x_i$ because $x_i^n=0$; quotienting by $(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$ gives $k$. Thus this fibre is a nonzero local ring with unique maximal ideal $(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$ and residue field $k$. The finite-over-henselian product theorem writes $B=\prod_{j=1}^s C_j$, with nonzero henselian local $R$-algebras $C_j$ and local structural maps. Each $C_j/\mathfrak m C_j$ is nonzero, because $\mathfrak m C_j$ lies in its maximal ideal. Therefore $s=1$: otherwise $B/\mathfrak m B$ would have a nontrivial factor idempotent, impossible in a local ring (for an idempotent $e$, either $e$ or $1-e$ is a unit, forcing $e=1$ or $e=0$). The case $s=0$ is excluded by the nonzero fibre. Hence $B$ is henselian local, its maximal ideal is $\mathfrak n=\mathfrak m B+(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$, and the residue map $k\to B/\mathfrak n$ is the identity under evaluation at all $x_i=0$. Since $k$ is separably closed, the definition makes $B$ strictly henselian.

source.place: Tag 04GH (lemma-finite-over-henselian), (1) and (2); Tag 04GF (definition-henselian), strictly henselian clause; explicit closed-fibre calculation.

proof.text: Extend the given parameters to $t_1,\ldots,t_r,t_{r+1},\ldots,t_d$, where $d=\dim R$ and these elements generate $\mathfrak m$. Then $\mathfrak n=(x_1,\ldots,x_r,t_{r+1},\ldots,t_d)$: the discarded generators $t_i=x_i^n$ already lie in $(x_i)$. Consequently the Noetherian local generator bound gives $\dim B\leq d$. Conversely take any strict chain $\mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak p_l$ in $R$. Lying over applies to the injective integral map of Step 1 and supplies $\mathfrak q_0$ over $\mathfrak p_0$. Repeated going up supplies $\mathfrak q_0\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathfrak q_l$ over the chain. Every inclusion is strict because the contractions are distinct. Taking suprema of chain lengths gives $\dim B\geq\dim R=d$. Thus $B$ has dimension $d$ and maximal ideal generated by $d$ elements, so is regular local by definition. Apply the regular-local-domain theorem to both $B$ and $R$, obtaining the domains used to form $E=\operatorname{Frac}(B)$ and $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$; the injection in Step 1 extends by $a/b\mapsto a/b$ to $K\hookrightarrow E$.

Let $\Gamma=(\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z)^r$. For $h\in\Gamma$, substitute $x_i\mapsto\zeta^{h_i}x_i$ and fix coefficients in $R$. This respects every equation because $(\zeta^{h_i}x_i)^n=t_i$, is independent of representatives because $\zeta^n=1$, and has inverse given by $-h$. The substitution therefore defines an $R$-algebra automorphism $\rho(h)$ of $B$. On fractions define $\rho(h)(b/c)=\rho(h)(b)/\rho(h)(c)$; cross multiplication proves well-definedness, and the inverse is still $\rho(-h)$. This fixes $K$ and gives a group homomorphism into $\operatorname{Aut}_K(E)$ because successive substitutions add the exponents. It is faithful: if $n>1$ and $h_i\neq0$, the difference $\rho(h)(x_i)-x_i=(\zeta^{h_i}-1)x_i$ has a nonzero coefficient in the monomial basis, since $\zeta^{h_i}-1$ is a unit of the nonzero ring $R$. Thus $\rho(h)\neq1$. For $n=1$ or $r=0$, $\Gamma$ is trivial and faithfulness holds directly.

proof.text: The fixed subring of this action on $B$ is precisely $R$. Indeed write $b=\sum_a c_a x^a$ in the basis of Step 1. For each coordinate $i$, rotation by the vector with $1$ in that coordinate multiplies the coefficient of $x^a$ by $\zeta^{a_i}$. If $b$ is fixed and $a_i\neq0$, uniqueness of expansion gives $(\zeta^{a_i}-1)c_a=0$, and the unit hypothesis forces $c_a=0$. Every nonzero exponent vector has such a coordinate, so only the constant coefficient remains. Constants are fixed by construction. When $n=1$ or $r=0$ the sole exponent vector is already zero, with the same conclusion.

proof.text:
The fixed field in $E$ is $K$, with no assumption about invariants commuting with localization. For $u=b/c\in E^\Gamma$ with $c
eq0$, set $D=\prod_{h\in\Gamma}ho(h)(c)$. Each factor is nonzero, so $D
eq0$ in the domain $B$; multiplication by a group element permutes the factors, so $D\in B^\Gamma=R$. The identity factor of this product is $c$, hence $M=b\prod_{h
eq0}ho(h)(c)$ belongs to $B$ and satisfies $M=uD$ in $E$. As $u$ and $D$ are fixed, $M$ is fixed, so $M\in R$ by Step 5. Therefore $u=M/D\in K$. The reverse inclusion follows because all rotations fix $R$ and hence its fractions.

proof.text: Apply the finite faithful field-action theorem to the field $E$, the finite group $\Gamma$ and the faithful homomorphism constructed in Step 4. Step 6 identifies its fixed field with the specified embedded $K$. The theorem gives that $E/K$ is finite-dimensional, separable algebraic and normal, and $[E:K]=|\Gamma|=n^r$. The finite-Galois automorphism theorem now gives $|\operatorname{Aut}_K(E)|=[E:K]=n^r$. Thus the injective homomorphism $\rho:\Gamma\to\operatorname{Aut}_K(E)$ is bijective, since its domain and codomain are finite of equal cardinality. This is the asserted group isomorphism with exactly the specified generator images. Its construction in Step 4 already proves that every such rotation preserves $B$.

source.place: Tag 09I3 (lemma-galois-over-fixed-field), Galois and degree clauses; Tag 09I1 (lemma-finite-Galois), automorphism cardinality.

proof.text: Put $A=R[1/f]$. The presentation of $B[1/f]$ over $A$ is $A[x_1,\ldots,x_r]/(x_i^n-t_i)$: localization and this quotient have the same universal property of roots together with an inverse for $f$. Each $t_i$ is a unit in $A$, with inverse $(\prod_{j\neq i}t_j)/f$. Adjoin the $x_i$ successively over $A$. At a stage $S$, put $C=S[T]/(Q)$ with $Q=T^n-t_i$ and root $x$. The equation makes $x$ a unit, with inverse $x^{n-1}/t_i$, so $Q'(x)=n x^{n-1}$ is a unit. The standard-etale algebra $S'=S[T,Y]/(Q,YQ'-1)$ is isomorphic to $C$: send $T$ to $x$ and $Y$ to $Q'(x)^{-1}$; conversely send $x$ to the class of $T$. The relation $YQ'=1$ makes the two maps inverse on $T,Y$ and coefficients. Thus the standard-etale theorem makes each $\operatorname{Spec}C\to\operatorname{Spec}S$ etale, and etale composition gives the desired etaleness. Repeated monic power bases give $B[1/f]$ a finite $A$-basis of the same monomials, proving finiteness of the affine morphism. For $r=0$ the map is the identity, also realized by the standard-etale presentation $Q=T$.

source.place: Tag 00UB (definition-standard-etale), Q=T^n-t_i; Tag 00UC (lemma-standard-etale); morphisms.tex Tag 02GN (lemma-composition-etale) and Tag 01WH (definition-integral).

proof.text: For $r=0$ the presentation has no variables or relations, so $B=R$, $f=1$, $E=K$, and $\Gamma$ is the trivial group; the basis consists of $1$ and $n^0=1$. For $n=1$ all relations are $x_i=t_i$, so again $B=R$ and $E=K$, the basis has only the zero exponent vector and the rotation group is trivial. All preceding arguments include these cases; in particular no division by $x_i$ or by a parameter was used before passing to the punctured algebra in Step 8.
